from pypdf import PdfReader

    chunks.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n\\n'+p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout'))
s=''.join(chunks)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(s)
print(s)

strengths: Addresses an important problem: retaining information beyond a transformer's context window in offline reinforcement learning, across both visual and vector observations.

The T-Maze results provide concrete evidence of long-horizon retention. After training on sequences of at most 150 steps, RATE achieves 0.90 ± 0.07 success at corridor length 900, compared with 0.61 ± 0.07 without MRV (Table 3).

Includes useful memory-randomization, component, curriculum, and memory-update ablations. Experiments span several memory-intensive environments, Atari games, and MuJoCo tasks, with substantial reported improvements on Breakout and Qbert.
Provides a code URL, environment and dataset descriptions, hyperparameter tables, and resource measurements. Reported GPU-memory reductions suggest practical value from segmented processing.
weaknesses: Novelty and comparative significance are insufficiently established. RATE combines existing recurrent memory tokens and Transformer-XL caching with standard cross-attention. The distinction from related memory-augmented decision transformers, including reference [28], needs clarification. Although component ablations are useful, the principal memory-task comparator is vanilla DT. Offline-trained recurrent policies, GTrXL-style models, and state-space alternatives are missing; replacing the MRV with an LSTM or GRU does not substitute for these policy baselines.

The training description contains a consequential contradiction. Section 3 says updated memory embeddings are detached, then says gradients flow through them into previous segments. If detachment is literal, subsequent action losses cannot train the MRV through that connection. The precise gradient truncation, hidden-state caching, and segment-update procedures must be specified to make the central method reproducible.

The MuJoCo evaluation confounds architecture with return conditioning. Appendix C resets the target return to its maximum at every segment, whereas baseline scores are imported from other papers. Without applying this strategy to DT and evaluating RATE without it, the reported improvements cannot be attributed specifically to recurrent memory.

The ViZDoom protocol does not clearly exclude alternative reward-based cues. Appendix A says rewards are withheld because they reveal the target color, but Section 3 supplies return-to-go values updated using observed rewards. Consecutive return-to-go values reveal those rewards. The paper needs to clarify any environment-specific exception and control this potential shortcut before interpreting performance as retention of the initial pillar cue.

Evidence for broader memory capabilities is weaker than the headline claims suggest. The clearest long-horizon results concern retaining a single cue or action. Memory Maze yields only 1.91 versus 1.45 rewards over 1,000 steps, with three training runs and no strong recurrent comparator. The detailed MRV-architecture comparison is confined to T-Maze, leaving its benefits for richer spatial memory and standard benchmarks insufficiently isolated.

Several quantitative claims require correction. Appendix C claims the best MuJoCo results on 5/9 tasks, but Table 2 gives RATE the highest mean on only 2/9. The claimed parameter increase of only embedding_dimension × memory_tokens also omits the learned MRV attention projections in Equations 4–6. These discrepancies weaken the performance and parameter-matching claims.
